_about.what: The war at sea. Fleets are counts of ships by class. A fleet on patrol holds a sea: it fights enemy fleets there, guards convoys and stops enemy troopships. A fleet raiding hunts merchant ships and avoids battle. A fleet in port is safe and refits.
_about.classes: power is a ship's weight in a fleet action. tough scales how likely it is to be sunk when its fleet takes losses (lower is tougher). escort is its worth guarding a convoy, raid its worth hunting one.
_about.quality: How well a navy fights, ship for ship.
_about.air: Aircraft flying from a sea's coasts count toward holding it. weight turns air strength into fleet strength. A surface fleet at sea where the enemy's air outweighs its own by more than 'safe' loses ships to bombers every month: lossPer of the fleet for each point beyond that, up to maxLoss. A computer-run admiral keeps out of water where the margin is over 'avoid'.
_about.closed: A sea is closed to a nation's troopships and supply ships when the enemy's strength there (ships at sea plus aircraft) is at least 'min' and at least 'ratio' times its own.
_about.ready: A fleet in harbour regains 'port' of its fitness for sea each month. On patrol it wears down to 'floor' and no further, and a damaged fleet that stays out mends only slowly. A battle costs the loser 'lost' and the winner 'won'. A computer-run fleet that has gone in to refit comes out again at sortieAt.
_about.battle: A patrolling fleet offers battle when it is at least 'seek' times as strong as the enemy in its sea. Raiding surface ships are brought to action with chance catchRaider. A fleet outnumbered by evadeAt or more slips away to port with chance evade.
_about.intercept: Troopships crossing a sea where enemy ships or aircraft are at work lose men: up to 'loss' of a corps when the enemy is unopposed. 'sea' is how hard a convoy is to find.
_about.landing: A corps landing on a defended coast fights at 'assault' strength; in the month war is declared the defenders are caught unready and it fights at 'surprise' strength and cannot be intercepted. range is how many seas a landing force can cross. Enemy fleets in harbour on those seas or the next ones put to sea against an invasion at 'sortie' of their strength. No landing can be made under a sky the enemy's fighters still hold, unless it is a surprise. Airborne troops (corps marked 'airborne' in the setup) need no ships and no open sea lane: once a month they can be flown from a friendly coast to an enemy one across a single sea, and fight there at 'airborne' strength, without heavy weapons.
_about.convoys: Routes that feed a nation by sea. The share of the cargo lost is raiders / (raiders + escorts x escortWorth + ocean); 'share' of the nation's production rides on the route, and 'tons' is the shipping sunk in a month if nothing got through. 'base' is a fortress astride the route: while an enemy of the route's owner holds it, its own submarines and aircraft hunt the convoys with strength 'raid', or 'starved' of that when it is cut off itself. What is sunk on the Libya route also lengthens the supply line of the armies in the desert: see desert.json.
_about.ore: Swedish iron ore reaches Germany across the Baltic when it is free of ice, and down the Norwegian coast from Narvik when it is not. If neither way is open, Germany loses 'share' of her production.
_about.fleets: The navies of 1 September 1939. base is the region of the home port (null for a base off the map, with 'home' naming the sea it opens on) and port its name. zone is the sea the fleet is stationed in and duty what it does there. 'from' brings a fleet into being later in the war.
_about.building: Ships that join a fleet every month over a span of turns.
_about.arrivals: Single ships that join a fleet in a given month: [turn, nation, fleet, ships, what the news calls them].
